content: 1. Before initiating treatment for chronic hepatitis B (CHB), it is essential to exclude other conditions such as fatty liver disease and dyslipidemia. 2. For individuals who do not meet any of the four established criteria for treatment eligibility, a person-centered approach should be adopted. This approach should consider individual circumstances and concerns, allowing flexibility to treat some individuals who fall outside the current treatment criteria. 3. Most individuals who do not meet treatment criteria have an HBV DNA viral load of less than 2000 IU/mL. This accounts for approximately 75% of HBsAg-positive individuals in sub-Saharan Africa and 50% in Asia. 4. Regardless of treatment status, this group requires ongoing monitoring to assess disease progression. 5. Annual monitoring for all individuals initiating treatment should include HBV DNA levels, ALT levels, and APRI scores, along with adherence support and retention in care. 6. Those not meeting treatment criteria also require continued monitoring to ensure timely intervention if disease progression occurs. 7. Patient preferences for initiating treatment vary. Among 550 individuals with CHB from 76 countries, the primary reasons for starting treatment included physician recommendation (30%), elevated HBV DNA levels (38%), and a desire to reduce the risk of liver cancer or liver damage (11%). 8. Reasons for not starting treatment included lack of physician recommendation (42%), high medication costs (23%), and feeling asymptomatic (11%). Only 4% expressed concerns about treatment side effects. 9. Patients also prioritized knowledgeable healthcare providers, confidentiality of test results, and shared decision-making regarding treatment initiation and management plans. 10. Approximately one-third of respondents were open to starting treatment on the same day of diagnosis (30%) or whenever their physician recommended it (50%). 11. A 2022 global survey of 178 healthcare workers found that 79% prioritized antiviral therapy for CHB patients with advanced hepatic fibrosis (stage 3 or 4). 12. Fifty-five percent supported treating individuals with elevated ALT levels regardless of HBV DNA levels, provided no other liver conditions were present. 13. Only 31% agreed with treating HBeAg-positive individuals with normal ALT levels, and 30% supported treating HBsAg-positive adults over 40 years old regardless of HBV DNA, HBeAg, or ALT levels. 14. A 2023 WHO survey of 32 national hepatitis program managers revealed that 55% supported treating all HBsAg-positive adults aged 30 or older with HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL, regardless of ALT levels. 15. Expanding treatment eligibility has cost implications that remain underexplored. Modeling studies are underway to assess the financial impact of expanded treatment in different regions, comparing treatment and monitoring costs under various scenarios. 16. The annual cost of treatment with generic tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) is low (approximately $30 annually), even over a lifetime of treatment. However, prices vary across lowand middle-income countries. 17. Long-term treatment with TDF or entecavir (ETV) requires laboratory infrastructure for monitoring ALT levels and, if possible, annual HBV DNA levels, which cost approximately $15–$60 annually. 18. Access to HBV DNA testing is improving in lowand middle-income countries but remains a significant barrier in rural areas and outside referral facilities. 19. Expanding and scaling up testing and case finding is a critical initial step. This includes routine testing of all pregnant women, family members, and children, along with vaccination of HBsAg-negative household contacts. 20. Individuals being considered for pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) should first be tested for HBV and HIV to ensure appropriate long-term management of CHB, HIV, or both. 21. Annual monitoring for all individuals initiating treatment should include HBV DNA, ALT, APRI scores, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) surveillance, along with adherence support and retention in care. 22. There are limited examples of expanded treatment eligibility adoption in lowand middle-income countries. For instance, Uzbekistan's experience showed that removing treatment restrictions did not necessarily increase treatment uptake, especially in areas with low awareness and acceptance. 23. Implementing expanded treatment eligibility poses significant challenges, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. It requires increased awareness, community education, expanded access to testing, trained healthcare personnel, and appropriate monitoring tools. 24. Initial assessment of CHB patients before therapy should include a detailed history, physical examination (including hepatomegaly and splenomegaly), and laboratory tests such as ALT, AST, ALP, total bilirubin, and full blood count. 25. Liver disease severity should be staged using APRI scores, calculated from AST and platelet count measurements. 26. Liver synthetic function should be assessed using serum albumin and prothrombin time or international normalized ratio (INR). 27. Patients should be evaluated for liver-related symptoms, although advanced disease may remain asymptomatic. 28. Viral replication should be assessed by quantifying serum HBV DNA and determining HBeAg and anti-HBe serostatus. 29. Comorbidities such as HIV, HCV, HDV coinfections, impaired glucose tolerance, dyslipidemia, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, alcoholic liver disease, and drug-induced liver injury should be assessed. 30. All individuals with cirrhosis should be screened for HCC. Family history of HCC and medication history should also be reviewed. 31. Household screening and preventive measures should include HBsAg testing and HBV vaccination for non-immune family and household members, as well as sexual contacts. 32. Lifestyle counseling should address alcohol consumption, diet, and physical activity, with advice on alcohol reduction, weight management, and avoiding sugar-sweetened beverages and ultra-processed foods. 33. HAV vaccination should be considered. 34. Management of individuals with steatosis and CHB includes liver fibrosis evaluation, antiviral therapy, and lifestyle modifications such as weight reduction, regular exercise, and correcting metabolic dysfunctions like diabetes, obesity, and dyslipidemia. 35. Counseling before treatment initiation should cover indications for treatment, potential benefits and side effects, the need for long-term adherence, and the risks of abrupt treatment discontinuation, which may lead to acute liver failure. 36. Baseline renal function should be assessed before initiating antiviral therapy, especially if a tenofovir-based regimen is used. This includes measuring serum creatinine levels and calculating estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). 37. Long-term studies are needed to evaluate the impact of expanded treatment eligibility on CHB-related morbidity and mortality, transmission reduction, quality of life, and economic burden. 38. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are required to establish the impact of antiviral therapy in individuals with low-level viraemia and early fibrosis stages, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. 39. Longitudinal studies should further evaluate ALT cut-offs and the prognostic significance of persistently normal ALT levels despite high HBV DNA levels in CHB patients. 40. The preferred antiviral regimens for CHB include tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) or entecavir (ETV), which have a high genetic barrier to resistance. Alternative regimens include TDF combined with lamivudine (3TC) or emtricitabine (FTC). 41. For individuals with osteoporosis or impaired kidney function, entecavir (ETV) or tenofovir alafenamide fumarate (TAF) is recommended. 42. For individuals coinfected with HIV and HBV, TDF (in combination with 3TC or FTC) is the preferred nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) backbone. TAF may be an alternative in cases of renal or bone concerns. 43. Antiviral therapy aims to prevent, reduce, or reverse necro-inflammatory changes and hepatic fibrosis, thereby reducing the risk of cirrhosis, liver failure, HCC, and death. 44. Treatment effectiveness is measured by normalization of ALT levels, reduction of HBV DNA to undetectable levels, HBeAg seroconversion, and improvement in hepatic fibrosis.
